summary: Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive website that turns the story of hardware people left on the Moon, Mars and in orbit into something you can explore. You can spin a real 3D Moon built from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data, move a timeline from 1966 to today, open story cards with photos and sources, or play a short Survival Simulator where you face the same decisions the engineers made with InSight, Spirit and Surveyor 3. details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive website about the machines people left behind on the Moon, on Mars, in Earth orbit and farther out. Some stopped working on purpose, some failed, some simply went silent. They’re still out there.

Instead of a list of facts, the site lets you explore them the way a mission control room would: you can spin a real 3D Moon built from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data, move a timeline from 1966 to today and watch each mission land, work, and go quiet. You can open story cards with photos, coordinates and sources, or play a Survival Simulator where you face the same decisions the real engineers made with InSight, Spirit and Surveyor 3.

How it works

Moon Mission Control — a 3D Moon from LRO data. Pins light up as you drag the year slider. Pip (the guide) reacts to what you tap.

Survival Simulator — three short campaigns based on real mission events. Your choices affect the outcome; at the end you see what NASA actually did and where the spacecraft is now.

Museum catalog — filterable story cards (retired hardware and lost missions) with 3D models and linked sources.

Atlas — real NASA map tiles (LRO WAC for the Moon, Viking/MOLA for Mars).

3D Lab — rotate official NASA public-domain models or simplified reconstructions.

Live Orbit — debris clouds positioned with real CelesTrak elements.

Ask Pip — a small chat that answers questions about the site using a knowledge base built from the project’s own data (and falls back to simple facts if the AI is down).

Why it’s creative

Most “space debris” projects show numbers or static maps. We turned the same material into something you can play and explore. The Survival Simulator doesn’t just tell you that dust killed InSight — it lets you try the real options (and see why some of them fail). The Moon view isn’t a picture; it’s data you can spin and travel through time with. The tone stays human and a little quiet — these are machines that stopped working, not heroes.

What we paid attention to

Accuracy: every event, date, coordinate and photo links to a NASA or peer-reviewed source. Gauge numbers in the game are clearly marked as a simplified model.

Audience: clear enough for students 11–15, still interesting for adults.

Accessibility: keyboard navigation, text descriptions for 3D views, reduced-motion support, optional sound.

Honesty about AI: Pip’s chat answers are AI-generated and can be wrong; the disclosure section says so and points people back to the sources.

No NASA logos or insignia in anything we made.

Tools & technologies

Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (Vite)

3D: Three.js (OrbitControls) + NASA 3D Resources models

Maps: Leaflet + NASA Solar System Treks / LRO / GIBS tiles

Orbit: satellite.js + CelesTrak data

Animation: GSAP + Lenis

AI chat: Supabase Edge Function proxy to OpenRouter (Nemotron / Gemma), with a local knowledge base generated from the site data

Other: Poly Haven CC0 textures, Fontsource fonts

Impact

The project makes abandoned hardware visible and personal. Instead of “there is a lot of junk in space,” a visitor can stand on the virtual Moon, open the story of Surveyor 3, and then play the decisions that kept (or didn’t keep) InSight alive.
